es.summary: Se creó o modificó un Job o CronJob de Kubernetes en un clúster AKS o en un clúster conectado con Azure Arc, mediante Azure Resource Manager. Puede ser una tarea administrativa legítima o un intento de programar código malicioso como persistencia.
es.what_it_detects: Eventos de Azure Activity Logs cuyo operationName empieza por MICROSOFT.CONTAINERSERVICE/MANAGEDCLUSTERS/BATCH o MICROSOFT.KUBERNETES/CONNECTEDCLUSTERS/BATCH y termina en /CRONJOBS/WRITE o /JOBS/WRITE.
es.why_it_matters: Un CronJob ejecuta contenedores de forma periódica y sobrevive a reinicios de pods. Un atacante puede usarlo para persistencia, ejecución recurrente o escalamiento de privilegios. La regla lo etiqueta como T1053.003 (Scheduled Task/Job: Cron).
triage_steps: Identifique el caller (usuario, service principal o managed identity), callerIpAddress y el resourceId del clúster afectado.
Confirme el operationName exacto (Job o CronJob), el estado de la operación y el correlationId.
Revise el manifiesto: kubectl get cronjob/job -n <namespace> -o yaml. Verifique imagen, comando, schedule, serviceAccount, privileged, hostPath y hostNetwork.
Valide que la imagen provenga de un registro aprobado y busque comandos sospechosos: descargas con curl/wget, shells reversos o mineros.
Busque en el Activity Log la actividad del mismo caller +/- 15 minutos: listClusterAdminCredential, role assignments y cambios de red.
Compare con tickets de cambio, pipelines de CI/CD y operaciones habituales de esa identidad en el clúster.
Revise los resource logs de AKS (kube-audit) para ver acciones por kubectl que no aparecen en el Activity Log.
Busque alertas previas del mismo caller, de la misma IP de origen o del mismo clúster.
false_positives: Administradores del clúster que crean Jobs o CronJobs desde el portal de Azure o con herramientas ARM.
Pipelines de CI/CD o herramientas GitOps que despliegan tareas batch programadas, como backups, limpiezas o reportes.
Comportamiento conocido y recurrente de una identidad específica, que puede exceptuarse de la regla.
response_steps: Verifique con el responsable del clúster o del caller si el cambio estaba autorizado antes de actuar.
Si no está autorizado, exporte el manifiesto y los logs de los pods como evidencia y suspenda el CronJob con spec.suspend=true.
Revoque sesiones y credenciales de la identidad comprometida y rote las credenciales del clúster.
Elimine el Job o CronJob malicioso y sus pods tras preservar la evidencia, y bloquee la imagen en el registro.
Busque otra persistencia en el clúster: DaemonSets, RoleBindings y secretos modificados. Luego restablezca la configuración aprobada.
es.severity_rationale: La severidad media es adecuada: la creación de Jobs es común en operaciones legítimas, pero en manos de un atacante ofrece ejecución y persistencia dentro del clúster.

en.summary: A Kubernetes Job or CronJob was created or modified through Azure Resource Manager on an AKS or Azure Arc-connected cluster. This may be routine admin work or an attempt to schedule malicious code for persistence.
en.what_it_detects: Azure Activity Log events whose operationName starts with MICROSOFT.CONTAINERSERVICE/MANAGEDCLUSTERS/BATCH or MICROSOFT.KUBERNETES/CONNECTEDCLUSTERS/BATCH and ends with /CRONJOBS/WRITE or /JOBS/WRITE.
en.why_it_matters: A CronJob runs containers on a schedule and survives pod restarts. Attackers can use one for persistence, repeated execution or privilege escalation. The rule tags it as T1053.003 (Scheduled Task/Job: Cron).
triage_steps: Identify the caller (user, service principal or managed identity), the callerIpAddress and the resourceId of the affected cluster.
Confirm the exact operationName (Job or CronJob), the operation status and the correlationId.
Inspect the manifest with kubectl get cronjob/job -n <namespace> -o yaml. Check the image, command, schedule, serviceAccount, privileged, hostPath and hostNetwork.
Make sure the image comes from an approved registry. Look for suspicious commands such as curl/wget downloads, reverse shells or miners.
Search the Activity Log for the same caller's activity within +/- 15 minutes: listClusterAdminCredential, role assignments and network changes.
Compare against change tickets, CI/CD pipelines and what this identity normally does on the cluster.
Review AKS resource logs (kube-audit) for kubectl actions, because those do not appear in the Activity Log.
Check for earlier alerts on the same caller, source IP or cluster.
false_positives: Cluster administrators creating Jobs or CronJobs from the Azure portal or with ARM tooling.
CI/CD pipelines or GitOps tools deploying scheduled batch tasks such as backups, cleanups or reports.
Known recurring behavior by a specific identity, which can be exempted from the rule.
response_steps: Before acting, confirm with the cluster owner or the caller's owner whether the change was authorized.
If it was not, export the manifest and pod logs as evidence, then suspend the CronJob by setting spec.suspend=true.
Revoke the compromised identity's sessions and credentials, and rotate the cluster credentials.
After preserving evidence, delete the malicious Job or CronJob and its pods, and block the image in the registry.
Hunt for other persistence in the cluster, such as DaemonSets, RoleBindings and modified secrets, then restore the approved configuration.
en.severity_rationale: Medium fits because creating Jobs is common in normal operations, but in an attacker's hands it gives execution and persistence inside the cluster.

positive.description: A user creates a CronJob on an AKS managed cluster through ARM
A service principal writes a Job on an Azure Arc-connected cluster

negative.description: A Deployment write on AKS: the operation is not under the batch resource path
A CronJob deletion: the batch prefix matches but the operation does not end in /WRITE
